explanation.headline: The change in your right eye is at NASA’s clinically concerning level.
summary: The larger increase is in your right eye: the retina next to the optic nerve is 60 µm thicker than in your own pre-flight exam (range 51 to 69), at or above NASA’s clinically concerning threshold of 55 µm.
The scan also indicates new folds in both eyes; NASA counts any fold as a first sign.
Today’s vision tests and answers add no finding.
Passing a threshold is not a diagnosis: most cases cause no symptoms, and your flight surgeon on the ground confirms the result and decides what to do.

OD.headline: Right eye: clinically concerning change, by NASA’s threshold.
lines: The retina next to your right optic nerve is 60 µm thicker than before the flight (range 51 to 69).
That is at or above NASA’s clinically concerning threshold of 55 µm.
It is likely (85 %) that the real change is at or above the clinically concerning threshold: this result is close to it, and your next exam will show whether it holds.
The scan indicates new folds: the waviness of the membrane under the retina rose by 5.8 µm since before the flight (range 3.6 to 8.0), above the limit of 2.8 µm.
It is very likely (more than 99 %) that the real change is above that limit; NASA counts any fold as a first sign.
Since your previous exam (flight day 118), it is 2 µm thicker (range: from 8 µm thinner to 13 µm thicker).

OS.headline: Left eye: first sign of optic nerve swelling, by NASA’s threshold.
lines: The retina next to your left optic nerve is 34 µm thicker than before the flight (range 24 to 45).
That is above NASA’s first-sign threshold of 19.4 µm and below its clinically concerning threshold of 55 µm.
It is very likely (more than 99 %) that the real change is above the first-sign threshold.
The scan indicates new folds: the waviness of the membrane under the retina rose by 3.9 µm since before the flight (range 1.7 to 6.1), above the limit of 2.8 µm.
It is likely (84 %) that the real change is above that limit; NASA counts any fold as a first sign.
Since your previous exam (flight day 118), it is 2 µm thicker (range: from 9 µm thinner to 12 µm thicker).

nextSteps.text: Tell your flight surgeon about this result without waiting for the routine report.
nextSteps.why: The change in your right eye is at NASA’s clinically concerning level, where NASA decides case by case what to do. Telling the flight surgeon early in these cases is this tool’s own rule: NASA’s is not public.

nextSteps.text: Repeat the scan of both eyes on flight day 150 (in 24 days).
nextSteps.why: At the clinically concerning level, this tool asks for the next scan 3 weeks later. That would be flight day 147; flight day 150 is a routine exam of NASA’s calendar and falls close to it, so one scan covers both. NASA does not publish how often to repeat the scan at this level. This interval is this tool’s own rule, based on the one published case, where the scan was repeated every 3 to 6 weeks.

nextSteps.text: Do the Amsler grid three times a week, one eye at a time.
nextSteps.why: Between scans, the grid can show a distortion at the centre of your vision. In the one published case it was used several times a week; this frequency is this tool’s own rule.

limitations.text: This is not a diagnosis: it is a first reading of a measurement against NASA’s published thresholds.
The exams in this demonstration are simulated; the analysis that measures them is real.
This tool has not been validated on people. Its ranges and probabilities come from a provisional error model that has not been measured yet.
Your flight surgeon on the ground confirms every result and has the final word.
The pressure inside the skull cannot be measured on board.
It does not measure the choroid, the layer of blood vessels under the retina.
It does not look at the macula, the centre of the retina: the scan covers only the area around the optic nerve.
It does not measure flattening of the back of the eye.
It does not measure a change in your glasses prescription: there is no reliable way to do that on board.

findings.text: The change in your right eye is at NASA’s clinically concerning level.
The change in your left eye is at NASA’s first-sign level.
The scan indicates new folds in both eyes.
